debugCheat.title: Debugging cheat sheet
debugCheat.intro: Every panel and the error messages from the levels, in a few lines each. Filter, click an example to copy it, or jump to the level that practises it.

read-trace.title: Read an error and its stack
read-trace.summary: The first line says what went wrong, the frames under it say where. The top frame is the line that threw; each frame below it is the line that called the one above. Start at the top, and if that code has always worked, step down to the call that handed it a wrong value. A link or frame opens its line in Code. A button that "does nothing" has usually thrown here: errors go to the Console, not to the page.

syntax.title: Syntax errors and the blank page
syntax.summary: A syntax error is found before any code runs, so no line of that module (or of any module that imports it) runs: the page is blank. It has no frames, only where the browser gave up, which is usually after the real mistake. Read the lines above it for a missing bracket; the indentation often gives it away.

input.title: The input line
input.summary: Type an expression at the bottom of the Console and press Enter: it runs inside the app. › is your input, ← the value as a one-line preview, and an error shows in red. Up and Down bring back your earlier inputs. Clear empties the Console, and so does a Reload. Look at the value first, then find out where it came from.

examples.0: What is it? A function, or an object that holds formatPrice and toCents?
examples.1: The type of a value
examples.2: Are two lines one object? true means one object under two names

await.title: Top-level await
await.summary: The input line accepts await, so you can see what a promise settles to without writing an async function. A rejection shows in red. const x = await … defines x for your later inputs.

examples.0: The price once the promise settles
examples.1: Without await you only see a Promise, not its value
examples.2: Keep the result for later inputs (it becomes a property of the window)

log.title: Log what you do not expect
log.summary: A catch that only says "failed" throws the real error away, and the Console stays quiet. Log it, or handle only the failures you know.

examples.0: Show the real error from a catch
examples.1: Label a value so you can find it in the Console

status.title: Status codes
status.summary: A status says whether the server understood the request. 2xx worked, 4xx means the request was wrong, 5xx means the server failed. The Network panel colours 2xx green and 4xx and 5xx red. Read the response body: the server often says what went wrong.

examples.0: Worked
examples.1: Saved a new thing (a POST). It can still have saved the wrong data
examples.2: The server refused what you sent: read its message in the response body
examples.3: Nothing lives at that address: the path is wrong
examples.4: The request clashes with the current state (the oven is already full)
examples.5: It arrived, but a field is not valid (a total that is not a number)
examples.6: The server crashed on it: look in its Logs
examples.7: The server cannot answer right now: try again later

no-code.title: Status words without a code
no-code.summary: When there is no answer the page can read, the Network panel shows a word instead of a code. The Console line above or below it says why.

examples.0: The request is still on its way
examples.1: The browser refused to let the page read the answer: the server sent no permission
examples.2: No answer at all (no connection); fetch rejects with "Failed to fetch"
examples.3: The page cancelled it, for example with controller.abort()

details.title: Request and response
details.summary: The panel lists requests in the order sent: method, name, status, time. Select one for its URL, Status, Time, Sent from (opens the line that sent it), and the headers and body of the Request and of the Response. Compare what the page sent with what the server built from it, and with the API description (api.md).

address.title: A 404 is a wrong address
address.summary: fetch does not fail on a 404: the server did answer. Compare the path in the Network panel with the paths the API really has, then follow it back (Sent from) to the line that builds the address.

examples.0: The path the API lists, not the old one

ok.title: Check response.ok
ok.summary: fetch rejects only when no answer arrives. A 404 or a 500 is an answer, so the promise resolves and response.ok is false. Check it right after the fetch, before you read the body as a success.

examples.0: Handle a failed answer before anything else
examples.1: Or look at the code itself

payload.title: Check the payload
payload.summary: When data arrives wrong, look at the request body in the Network panel first: it tells you whether the page sent the wrong thing or the server read it wrong. JSON keeps types: "3" and 3 are different for the server, and a field the server does not know is usually ignored without a word.

examples.0: Form fields give text: send a number as a number

cors.title: CORS
cors.summary: A page may send a request to another origin, but may read the answer only if that server allows it. Without an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header for the page's origin (or *), the browser hides the answer and fetch fails with "Failed to fetch"; the reason is in the Console. It works in curl or Postman because they are not browsers. Fix it on the server, never in the page, or send the call to your own origin, which forwards it.

examples.0: What the other server has to send
examples.1: Same origin: no CORS check at all

double.title: Two POSTs for one click
double.summary: A slow answer invites a second click, and the browser sends what the code says: two clicks, two requests. Ignore clicks while a request is on its way and turn the button back on when the answer is in. This only makes duplicates rarer: a server that takes money also needs a unique id per order (an idempotency key).

examples.0: Ignore clicks while it sends

tree.title: The tree and Refresh
tree.summary: The tree shows the page as markup. It is a snapshot: press Refresh to see the page as it is now. An element without a box is dimmed ("not shown"), and one whose content is wider than its box gets a scroll badge. Keys: Up and Down, Home and End, Right and Left open and close.

styles.title: Matched rules and overridden declarations
styles.summary: Styles lists element.style, then the rules that match from the winner down, each with its media query, its selector, its specificity and where it is written (a link to the line). A declaration struck through lost to a stronger one; one with a warning is refused by the browser. A property that nothing else sets stays active, which is how a price can get bold but not red.

specificity.title: Specificity
specificity.summary: When two rules set the same property, the browser compares selectors: ids first, then classes (and attributes and pseudo-classes), then element names. The panel shows it as ids · classes · types. The order in the file only breaks a tie. Match the specificity or lower the old rule; !important just starts an arms race.

examples.0: 1 · 1 · 0: the id wins over any number of classes
examples.1: 0 · 2 · 0: loses to the rule above, even if it comes later
examples.2: 0 · 2 · 0: ties with the one above, so the later rule wins

variables.title: Variables that are not defined
variables.summary: var(--name) with no such property makes the declaration invalid at computed-value time, and the browser reports it nowhere. The property then behaves as if it were not set: a property that is not inherited, like background, gets its starting value (transparent), while an inherited one, like color, takes its parent's value. The panel marks it "--brown is not defined" under the declaration. Look at the :root rule under Inherited from for the real names.

examples.0: An invisible button: the variable does not exist

computed.title: Computed values and contrast
computed.summary: Computed is what the page really gets; the rules show how it got there. It lists display, visibility, opacity, position, z-index, pointer-events, color, background-color, width, height, min-width, overflow, text-overflow and white-space. Invisible is not gone: text and background of the same colour keep their box, so Pick can still select it. Normal text needs a contrast of at least 4.5 : 1.

pick.title: Pick mode
pick.summary: Pick, then click in the app: the element that is really under the pointer is selected (the app never gets that click), the tree opens to it, and hovering outlines it. Escape stops. It shows what a tap lands on, so when a button "does nothing" without an error, pick it: something invisible may sit on top.

covered.title: Something on top of the button
covered.summary: The browser sends a click to the topmost element under the pointer. A transparent box with a higher z-index takes every tap meant for what is below. Let clicks pass through it, or stack or move it differently. Nothing invisible should sit on top of a button.

examples.0: The element ignores the pointer, and so do its children
examples.1: Children that need clicks (a toast) switch it on again
examples.2: Stacked above: check which one has the higher value

box.title: The box and what sticks out
box.summary: Box shows margin, border, padding and content with their sides (a dash for 0), and says "Its content is 512 px wide in a 340 px box: it sticks out." when it does. A flex item will not get narrower than its content unless you allow it, and white-space: nowrap makes that content the whole text.

examples.0: Let a flex item shrink below its content
examples.1: Cut a long text with a "…" (with overflow: hidden and white-space: nowrap)
examples.2: Let a long word or address break

media.title: Media queries
media.summary: A media query is a condition on the width of the page, not on the device. Elements lists only the rules whose query holds right now, and the App shows its width next to the address. Test a layout change at both ends: a phone and a laptop width.

examples.0: Holds from 600 px wide and up: not "on desktop"
examples.1: Holds up to 600 px wide

missing-await.title: Missing await
missing-await.summary: Calling an async function gives you a promise at once, not the result. Written into the page it reads [object Promise]; used as a list it throws "map is not a function" or "is not iterable". await waits for the result: inside an async function, or at the top level of a module. In the Console a promise shows as a Promise, not as its value.

examples.0: Wait for the result
examples.1: Or continue in a then

race.title: Races and AbortController
race.summary: Two requests are on their way and the newer one answers first, so the old answer arrives last and wins. It only happens sometimes. Decide what is still wanted when an answer arrives, or cancel the old request. An aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError (the Network panel says canceled), so catch it and ignore it. A debounce sends fewer requests but does not fix the race.

examples.0: A counter: take a ticket per request
examples.1: Drop the answer when a newer request has started
examples.2: Cancel the old request, if there is one
examples.3: A new controller for the new request
examples.4: Give the request the controller's signal
examples.5: An abort on purpose is not an error

closure.title: Closures and var in a loop
closure.summary: A function made in a loop keeps the variables themselves, not a copy of their values, and reads them when it runs, long after the loop. var belongs to the whole function, so every handler shares one variable and sees the last value. let and const make a fresh one per round.

examples.0: Each round gets its own product
examples.1: Or a callback parameter, which is new for every call

copy.title: Shallow copies
copy.summary: A variable holds a reference to an object, not the object. A spread copies the top level only, so a nested object stays shared and changing one thing changes the other. Check with === in the Console: true means one object. Object.assign is shallow too.

examples.0: Copy everything
examples.1: Copy the nested object as well
examples.2: Or never edit the shared one: replace it

chain.title: Promise chains that lose their value
chain.summary: Each then hands the next one what its callback returns. A callback that returns nothing passes undefined on, and the next one throws. A catch that treats every error as "the server said no" hides the real one. With async and await the code reads top to bottom and nothing can be forgotten between the steps.

examples.0: Return it, or the next then gets undefined
examples.1: The same with await, and one try and catch around it
examples.2: A catch tells you what it does not expect

record.title: Record, then step
record.summary: The Debugger records a run: press Record, use the app, press Stop. The app is never paused: you move through what it already did and see each value as it was then, so you can go back as well as forward. Edited the code? Save, then Record again. A Reload, Reset or Again ends a recording. It opens at the first step a breakpoint stops at.

breakpoints.title: Breakpoints
breakpoints.summary: Click the gutter in Code (Ctrl or Cmd+B, or Breakpoint here in the panel, work without the mouse). Each breakpoint is listed with its line and how often it stopped in the recording ("hit 2 times", "not hit"); a breakpoint that stopped twice for one action shows that something runs twice. Remove it from its list. The breakpoints stay while you are on the page.

condition.title: Conditional breakpoints
condition.summary: Give a breakpoint a condition (the field under it: Enter or leaving it sets it) and it stops only where the condition holds, checked on the values each round had. That finds the one odd row of a thousand. A condition that cannot be read shows why under the field.

examples.0: Stop on the cheap row
examples.1: Stop on the bread with the odd weight
examples.2: Stop on one named item

stepping.title: Step over, into, out and back
stepping.summary: Resume goes to the next breakpoint (with none ahead, to the end). Step over runs the line, Step into goes inside the function it calls, Step out runs to the end of the current function. Step back and Back to the previous breakpoint go the other way. The scrubber shows "Step 37 of 412". Stepping over a line and comparing the Scope before and after shows what it changed.

shortcuts.title: Shortcuts
shortcuts.summary: The keys DevTools uses, while there is a recording and no dialog is open. Step back and Back to the previous breakpoint have no key. Plain F11 stays the browser's full screen.

examples.0: Resume
examples.1: Step over
examples.2: Step into

scope.title: Scope
scope.summary: Scope lists the variables of the current step: Block, Local (with this), Closure and Module. Values look like the browser's preview: strings green, numbers and booleans amber, undefined and null dimmed, functions blue; an object opens. It shows the raw value, with every digit, which is what the code compares: 24.999999999999996 shows as 25.00 on the page. When what the page shows and what the code decides disagree, put a breakpoint where it decides.

stack.title: Call stack
stack.summary: The frames of the current step, top first, each with its function and file:line. Click a frame to see its line in Code and its variables at that moment: the way to find out who called a function, and each time. An "async" line marks the call that started an async function now back from an await.

units.title: Counted, not timed
units.summary: The Performance panel counts: one unit of work is one statement of the app's code that ran (a built-in like sort or toFixed counts as part of the statement that calls it), and request times are the server's scripted delays. The same run shows the same numbers on every computer. Record, use the app, Stop. Show picks the whole recording or one action; the totals are Work, Renders, Requests and Server time.

functions.title: Functions: calls, self and total
functions.summary: Calls is how often a function ran. Self is its own statements, Total is itself and everything it called. A function with a big total and a small self spends its time in what it calls. A huge number of calls of a small function means work inside a loop that does not depend on the round: do it once, outside, or look it up in a Map.

renders.title: Renders and nodes
renders.summary: A render is a call of a function that changed the page; its nodes are the elements and texts it added, removed or changed. One Add should cost the basket a few nodes, not the whole menu 48. Draw again only the part whose data changed (a framework does that bookkeeping for you).

requests.title: Requests over time
requests.summary: Each request has a bar from its start to its end. "Sent once menu answered" marks a waterfall: it waited for another answer though it did not need it. "The same request again" marks an answer that was thrown away. A request per key typed is the third thing to look for.

examples.0: Start them together and wait for all
examples.1: A debounce: each key cancels the timer of the key before
examples.2: A cache by name; keeping the promise also covers a second click

logs.title: Logs
logs.summary: The Logs panel is the server's own story: time on the server's clock, level, route, request id, message and the stack where it failed. Filter by level or by text. A page that shows the server's reference for a failed request (x-request-id) gives you the id to search for; an id of this load links to that request in Network. Compare when the first failure came with when things last worked.

examples.0: Filter on a request id

deploys.title: Deploys and diffs
deploys.summary: Deploys lists the versions newest first: id, who and when, the message, and the live one. "Changes in …" opens the diff per file: added lines green, removed lines red, with their line numbers; a changed line opens in Code. Read the diff for who else uses what changed: damage is often in a file the deploy never touched.

which.title: Which deploy broke it?
which.summary: Put the timeline from the Logs next to the list of deploys: the last good request, the first failure, the deploy in between. With several suspects, bisect: roll back to the middle, check the shop, keep halving.

rollback.title: Roll back
rollback.summary: Roll back to a version sends your saved code back to it (Reload runs it), after asking what changes, which saved changes of your own are replaced and which unsaved edits are dropped. Go back to the last version that worked and no further, then check what it changes and check the shop. Back to live returns to the newest version, and Undo roll back brings your replaced changes back, until you save again. Roll back when you do not know the cause yet or the fix takes longer than customers can wait; with a clear one-line cause, fix forward.

flags.title: Feature flags
flags.summary: A feature flag switches a feature on or off from configuration, so you can turn it off without another deploy. When code behaves differently in one environment, look at the flags it picked: here the deploy named them "live" while the script calls the environment "production", and a fallback quietly handed production the staging flags. Fail loudly instead of falling back.

examples.0: Look up the flags by the environment's name
examples.1: A missing name should stop the page, not hide

json.title: Never build JSON or HTML by hand
json.summary: Gluing text into JSON breaks on exactly the characters JSON gives a meaning to: a quote, a line break, a backslash. Failures that hit only some customers often share such a character: put the failed requests side by side in the Logs. Let JSON.stringify escape it; the same goes for textContent instead of innerHTML. Test with the input real people type.

examples.0: The server reads the note exactly as typed
examples.1: Text stays text in the page

cannot-read.means: The thing before the dot is undefined (or null). The message names what you tried to read, not the mistake, which is a step earlier.
cannot-read.look: The top frame's line and the name just before the dot: often a misspelled property (cart.itmes) or data that has not arrived. Type that name in the Console input.

not-a-function.means: What you called is not a function: an object, undefined, a promise. The function is not missing.
not-a-function.look: Type the name in the Console input and read its value, then check its import: braces take a named export, no braces the default one.

wrong-value.means: A helper got a value of the wrong kind (here the whole cart instead of a number). The helper is usually right.
wrong-value.look: Step down the stack to the frame that called it and see what it passed. Fix it there, not in the helper.

map-not-a-function.means: An array method on something that is not an array. Often a promise, because an await is missing, or an object.
map-not-a-function.look: Type the name in the Console: a Promise instead of the value means a missing await.

not-iterable.means: A for…of, spread or destructuring got something that is not a list: undefined, an object or a promise. In a promise chain, the step before returned nothing.
not-iterable.look: What did the step before return? Each then passes on only what its callback returns.

not-defined.means: No variable of that name is in reach at that line: misspelled, declared in another block (let and const stay between their braces) or never imported.
not-defined.look: Find where it is declared and ask whether that place is in reach of the line in the trace.

before-init.means: A let or const used on a line before the one that declares it.
before-init.look: Move the declaration above its first use.

unexpected-export.means: A syntax error: the browser gave up here, usually a few lines after the real mistake, often a missing bracket. Nothing in that module runs, so the page is blank.
unexpected-export.look: Read the lines above the reported one; look at the indentation for the missing closing brace.

missing-export.means: A named import the module does not export (renamed, or it only has a default export). Nothing in the module graph runs.
missing-export.look: Open the imported file and compare its export names; an import with as keeps the old name in your file.

not-json.means: response.json() got HTML, not JSON: usually the server's error page, because of a wrong address or a server error.
not-json.look: The Network panel: the request's status and the body that came back, before you read any code.

not-found.means: The browser's own line for a failed request. The server answered, but has nothing at that address.
not-found.look: Compare the path with the paths the API lists (api.md); Sent from opens the line that built the address.

failed-fetch.means: No answer the page may read: the browser blocked it (CORS) or there is no connection. It is not an HTTP status.
failed-fetch.look: The line above it in the Console, and the status in Network: CORS error or failed.

cors-blocked.means: The other server did not say your page may read its answer. It is fixed on that server, or by calling your own origin, never in the page.
cors-blocked.look: Which origin and which header the message names; then the request's status (CORS error) in Network.

aborted.means: A fetch was cancelled with controller.abort(): the Network panel says canceled. Expected when you cancel on purpose.
aborted.look: Catch AbortError and ignore it, so the Console only shows real errors.

about.title: Practice the skills you use every day
about.intro: Grindstone is a training ground for developers: short, game-like levels that run in your browser. The first track is git, because everyone uses it and almost everyone is a little afraid of rebase.

teammates.title: You are not alone in the repo
teammates.text: Simulated teammates push to origin while you work. Keeping your branch in sync, rebasing onto a moved main and force-pushing safely only make sense when others change things too.

real.title: It feels like the real thing
real.text: Commands and messages follow real git, down to "rejected, fetch first". What you practise here carries over to your own terminal.

graph.title: You see what git does
graph.text: Every command redraws a live commit graph, so branches, merges and rebases stop being invisible.

ide.title: Work the way you work
ide.text: Use a plain terminal, or an IDE layout with files, an editor with conflict actions and a terminal below.

about.how: Everything runs in your browser: Grindstone has its own git simulation in TypeScript, so levels are predictable, undo is instant and what you type never leaves your browser. Debugging levels run a small real app in a sealed frame that can't see Grindstone, your progress or the network. Your progress stays on your device. To see which levels are too hard, Grindstone counts visits and which levels are started and solved, anonymously and without cookies, on its own server (Umami). If your browser sends Do Not Track, nothing is counted. The code is open source.

later.tracks: More tracks: working with AI, web fundamentals, framework deep dives
later.profile: A skill profile that shows where you are strong and what to practise next

about.by: Grindstone is built by Dominik Kiessling, a frontend and full-stack developer working with Vue, Nuxt and TypeScript.

debugger.label: Debugger
debugger.intro: Record a run: the app reloads with its code instrumented, you use it (click Add, tick a box…), then press Stop. Then step through what it did, forward and back, with every variable's value at each moment. Set breakpoints first or later: click a line number in Code, or press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B) on a line.
debugger.recording: Recording: use the app (click Add, tick a box…), then press Stop. Every line that runs is recorded with its values.
debugger.recorded: Recorded run: the app isn't paused. You move through what it already did, and see each value as it was then.

ended.steps: The recording stopped after {n} steps, the most it keeps. Record again and do less, or step from the start.
ended.slow: The recording stopped: reading the app's values took too long. What it recorded until then is here.

debugger.outdated: The code changed since this recording, so its lines may not match. Save, then Record again to step through the new code.

skipped.syntax: {path} could not be read (a syntax error): it ran without steps.
skipped.size: {path} is too long to record: it ran without steps.
skipped.nesting: {path} is nested too deeply to record: it ran without steps.
skipped.names: {path} uses the recorder's own name: it ran without steps.
skipped.points: {path} has more statements than a recording keeps: it ran without steps.
skipped.clash: {path} declares a function twice, or a var with a function's name, in one function, which a recording can't keep apart: it ran without steps.

debugger.empty: Nothing was recorded: no line of the app ran while recording.
debugger.toolsFailed: The Debugger's tools could not be loaded (are you offline?). Check your connection and try again.

note.noBreakpointAhead: No breakpoint stops after this: at the end of the recording.
note.noBreakpointBehind: No breakpoint stops before this: at the start of the recording.

debugger.noBreakpoints: No breakpoints. Click a line number in Code, or press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B) on a line, to set one.
debugger.hits: not hit | hit once | hit {n} times

debugging.performanceNote: Record a run of the app and see what it costs, then fix the code, Save and Reload: the goals are checked on every reload.

performance.label: Performance
performance.intro: Record a run: the app reloads with its code counted, you use it (type in the search, click Add…), then press Stop. Then see how often each function ran and how much work it did, what it changed on the page, and when its requests went out.
performance.recording: Recording: use the app (type, click Add…), then press Stop. Every statement that runs is counted.
performance.recorded: Counted, not timed: one unit of work is one statement of the app's code that ran (a built-in like sort or toFixed counts as part of the statement that calls it), and request times are the server's scripted delays. So the same run shows the same numbers on every computer.
performance.ended: Counting stopped after {n} units, the most it counts. The app ran on; what it did until then is here.
performance.outdated: The code changed since this recording, so its lines may not match. Save, then Record again to count the new code.
performance.empty: Nothing was counted: the profile did not arrive. Record again.
performance.toolsFailed: The Performance panel's tools could not be loaded (are you offline?). Check your connection and try again.

skipped.syntax: {path} could not be read (a syntax error): it ran without counting.
skipped.size: {path} is too long to count: it ran without counting.
skipped.nesting: {path} is nested too deeply to count: it ran without counting.
skipped.names: {path} uses the recorder's own name: it ran without counting.
skipped.points: {path} has more statements than can be counted: it ran without counting.
skipped.clash: {path} declares a function twice, or a var with a function's name, in one function: it ran without counting.

performance.actionsNote: An action counts everything that ran from it until the next one, answers that arrive meanwhile included.
performance.functionsNote: Most work first. Self: the function's own statements; total: with everything it called.
performance.noFunctions: No code of the app ran here.
performance.rendersNote: A render is a call of a function that changed the page; nodes are the elements and texts it added, removed or changed. Each line that did it is listed under it.
performance.noRenders: Nothing on the page changed here.
performance.requestsNote: On the server's clock: each bar runs from when the code sent the request to when its answer arrived.
